question: Am I sinful for refusing my parents when they pressure me to divorce my wife?
asked: He got married, and now his parents are having issues with his wife and are strongly pressuring him to divorce her. They mention that Ibn Umar was told by his father Umar ibn al-Khattab to divorce his wife, and he ended up divorcing her. Is he sinful for not obeying his parents, since he wishes to remain with his wife?
answer:
SubhanAllah, where does one begin? This is one of our biggest issues and problems when it comes to marriage: the in-laws of both sides. Sometimes they interfere too much, and parents want to live their dreams through their children, not realizing that their children are no longer children, not realizing that their children are now adults, not realizing that they themselves would never have accepted such interference when they were at that age.

And this, subhanAllah, is the bane of humanity. As the saying goes, every mother-in-law at one point in time was in fact a daughter-in-law. And yet when the tables turn, a lot of times it changes. And the same goes for the father as well: every father-in-law was at one point in time a son-in-law. But subhanAllah, this is Allah's qadar and our weakness of humanity. SubhanAllah, how quickly we forget. When we are in positions of weakness we think and act differently; when we get to positions of power, we forget. And this is the general rule. It's not just a father-in-law or mother-in-law; it's even when it comes to politicians, and kings or princes, or rich versus poor. We forget how it used to be, and now we get a sense of arrogance and pride and whatnot. So this is our weakness; we ask Allah's forgiveness.

Now, the son is saying that the parents are putting pressure on him, that obedience to the parents is obligatory. Indeed, obedience to the parents is generally obligatory, no question about that. However: generally, not unconditionally. Our Prophet ﷺ said there is no obedience to a created being when it comes to disobeying one of the rights of Allah.

You have to realize, dear husband, that now you have the rights of your father and mother, and you have the rights of another lady that you have married, who is called your wife. You cannot ignore any of these rights at the expense of the others. You have to balance all of these rights. You cannot neglect the rights of your parents, but neither can the rights of your parents infringe on the rights of your spouse, because each one now has a haqq on you.

Shaykh Ibn Taymiyyah says in his famous book Al-Ikhtiyarat, a famous book of principles of fiqh, of what he has chosen in fiqh, fiqh maxims: it is obligatory on every person to listen to his parents whenever it does not involve a sin, even if the parents are not righteous. However, listen to Ibn Taymiyyah: this is when they command the child or the son to do something that will be beneficial to them and not harmful to him.

So when the parents say, "We don't have anybody to help us bring food to our house," it is obligatory for the son or daughter to figure out how to bring food to them. If they cannot go outside, how to take care of them, if he's able to do so: this becomes wajib, because this is a benefit to them and there's no immediate harm on him. But when the parents command something that is harmful to the son or daughter, and there's no benefit going back to them immediately, in this case it is not obligatory to listen to the parents.

The parents are not unconditional. They're not, a'udhu billah, walking gods, where whatever they say you must listen to. No, the parents have a reasonable right of obedience. If it becomes unreasonable, we do not pay attention to the parents. And therefore, if they are asking for something unreasonable... and generally speaking, generally speaking, the parents getting involved in the marriage is unreasonable. This is the default. This is just the default; there might be some exceptions. Sometimes a spouse is very abusive and the other spouse doesn't see it, and the parents and relatives are all saying to the spouse, "Hey, you need to get out, you need to do that," and for whatever reason he or she doesn't see this. So that's a different thing.

But the default is that the reasons that the parents have are not... Who cares if the parents don't like the spouse? The marriage has taken place, there might be children involved, and it's the two who are living together who actually have to deal with the primary repercussions of each other. So if a third party, an uncle, an aunt, a parent, comes and says, "I don't like the spouse": okay, you only visit once a week, once a month, once a year. It's the two of them that have to live together. And therefore they do not have to listen to the parents in this regard.

In fact, as for this issue of Ibn Umar and Umar ibn al-Khattab, this is a famous, famous incident. Indeed, it did happen. But Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal was asked about this exact issue: a man came and said, "My father wants me to divorce my wife, and my father is quoting Umar about his son Ibn Umar." Because it did happen that Umar ibn al-Khattab had an issue with his daughter-in-law, and we don't know the details, and the Prophet ﷺ sided with the father and said to divorce her. So we don't know the details of that, but there is no doubt that the reason must have been an Islamic one, not "I don't like the lady." There must have been an Islamic reason that, for whatever reason, Ibn Umar was not seeing, and therefore he was told to divorce.

When Imam Ahmad was asked about this exact same scenario, he basically said to him, and I'm paraphrasing: when you have a father like Umar ibn al-Khattab, then you listen to him. Your father is not Umar ibn al-Khattab. The level of knowledge and taqwa and iman that your father has, there is no comparison. So when your father becomes Umar ibn al-Khattab, then you listen to Umar ibn al-Khattab to divorce your wife.

Otherwise, if we were to open this door, dear brothers and sisters, no marriage on earth would remain. Because it is the default in our human weakness, subhanAllah, that parents are not satisfied with the spouses of their children, even if they have chosen them, by the way. Why? Because they think, "My son deserves better, my daughter deserved better." This is their own standard. This is human nature: "Oh, we were better than this. He could have had somebody, or she could have had somebody better." SubhanAllah, it's not your life to live anymore. It's not your life.

One of our biggest problems is parents interfering in the marriages of their children, thinking that their children are children. They are no longer children; they are now full-fledged adults. Once they are married, they're standing on their own feet. It's not your business to interfere.

Yes, if there is genuine harm, or an un-Islamic character, or something of this nature, you should explain the reason. Explain that this is harmful to you, to your health; he or she is abusing you; he or she is doing something that is not good for Islam, going behind your back and doing something that's going to harm you, etc. Explain your reasons, and then bring other people in as well. Don't just say, "I don't like the girl, I don't like the boy, he's not good enough." That's not your business to decide now. The marriage has taken place, and it is their life to live.

And therefore, dear brother Talat, **you do not have to listen to your parents when it comes to this issue.** It is not obligatory to listen to your parents when they're asking for that which is unreasonable, or that which is harmful to you and to your other obligations. And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
